what_its_for: Enalapril is used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) and heart failure. It helps your heart pump blood more easily by relaxing and widening your blood vessels. This can lower your blood pressure, reduce strain on your heart, and help prevent heart attacks, strokes, and kidney problems.
how_to_take: Take enalapril by mouth with or without food. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. Try to take it at the same time each day so it becomes part of your daily routine. If you are using the liquid form (Epaned), shake the bottle well before measuring your dose and use the measuring device that came with your medicine — never use a regular kitchen spoon.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your condition and how well your body responds to the medicine. Most adults start at a low dose (2.5 to 5 mg once or twice daily) and the dose may be slowly increased over time. Always follow your doctor's instructions and never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — unless it is almost time for your next scheduled dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store enalapril tablets at room temperature, away from heat, light, and moisture. Keep it out of the bathroom medicine cabinet. Store the liquid form (Epaned) in the refrigerator and use it within 60 days of opening. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid using salt substitutes or potassium supplements unless your doctor tells you it is okay, as enalapril can raise potassium levels in your blood. Limit alcohol, as it can lower your blood pressure too much and cause dizziness. Avoid taking NSAIDs (like ibuprofen or naproxen) regularly without checking with your doctor, as they can reduce how well enalapril works and harm your kidneys. Be careful when standing up quickly, especially in hot weather or after exercise, as you may feel dizzy. Do NOT take enalapril if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant — it can seriously harm an unborn baby.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency help if you notice: sudden swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat (this is called angioedema and is a serious allergic reaction); trouble breathing or swallowing; severe dizziness or fainting; chest pain; signs of high potassium such as muscle weakness or irregular heartbeat; decreased urination or signs of kidney problems; a dry, persistent cough that bothers you (this is a common side effect — your doctor may switch your medication); or if you think you might be pregnant.
when_it_works: You may start to notice your blood pressure going down within a few hours of taking your first dose. However, it may take 1 to 2 weeks of regular use before you feel the full benefits. Even if you feel well, keep taking enalapril every day as prescribed — high blood pressure often has no symptoms, and stopping suddenly can be harmful.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Do NOT use enalapril during pregnancy. It can cause serious harm or death to an unborn baby. Tell your doctor immediately if you become pregnant. Breastfeeding: Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding while taking this medicine. Elderly patients: Older adults may be more sensitive to the blood pressure-lowering effects and dizziness — use caution when standing up. Kidney disease: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose or monitor you more closely. Children: Enalapril can be used in children for high blood pressure, but the dose will be carefully calculated based on body weight — always follow your pediatrician's instructions.
